newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Justice announces new Unabomber indictment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Justice announces new Unabomber indictment.

text.p: Theodore Kaczynski, already charged in a number of attacks attributed to the so-called Unabomber, was indicted on Tuesday for a 1994 bombing that killed a New Jersey advertising executive, the Justice Department said.
The three-count indictment was issued by a federal grand jury in Newark, but the Justice Department said it planned to proceed first with the pending criminal case against Kaczynski in California.

The new charges alleged that Kaczynski, a brilliant former mathematics professor turned recluse, mailed the parcel bomb that killed advertising executive Thomas Mosser on December 10, 1994 at his home in North Caldwell, New Jersey.
Kaczynski allegedly transported the bomb from Montana, where he lived in a one-room shack, to San Francisco, where he mailed it. When Mosser opened the package, it exploded, killing him instantly.
The latest charges carry a maximum sentence of the death penalty, which prosecutors also could seek in the California case.
The FBI believes that Kaczynski, 54, was responsible for the string of mail bomb attacks that killed three people and injured 23 since 1978.
A Justice Department prosecutor told a court hearing in Sacramento, California, last month that Kaczynski kept detailed journals in which he admitted each of the 16 bombings linked to the Unabomber.
On June 18 a federal grand jury in Sacramento returned a 10-count indictment against Kaczynski charging him with four separate bomb attacks that killed two persons and injured two others.
Kaczynski, held in jail without bond since his arrest in April, pleaded not guilty to those charges and was awaiting trial.
Later in June the Justice Department announced that four new indictments had been unsealed charging Kaczynski in three more bombings in Utah, Tennessee and Michigan in the 1980s.

In the New Jersey case, Kaczynski was charged with transporting an explosive with intent to kill or injure, mailing an explosive device with the same purpose and using a destructive device for a crime of violence.

The FBI dubbed the bomber the Unabomber because universities and airlines were the first targets. After a long investigation the FBI began to focus on Kaczynski after his brother in January went to the agency with his suspicions.

Among the items found in Kaczynski's cabin were an original copy of the Unabomber's rambling anti-technology manifesto, a typewriter used to write it, a bomb, a partially completed bomb and bomb-making parts, FBI officials have said.
